title: WHAT THE DATA SAY: Gen Z embracing religion at nearly double rate of parents, grandparents
body_markdown:
By: Ray Day


## **CONTACT:**


Ray Day
ray.day@stagwellglobal.com


*We wanted to share our latest consumer and business insights, based on research from[Stagwell](https://www.stagwellglobal.com/) and[Allison Worldwide](https://www.allisonworldwide.com/) .* *Among the highlights of our weekly* *consumer sentiment tracking:*


**GEN Z MORE RELIGIOUS THAN PARENTS**


Gen Z is embracing religion at nearly double the rate of Baby Boomers, based on new[Harris Poll research](https://theharrispoll.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/The-Gen-Z-and-Religion-Report-September-2026-1.pdf) .


- 33% of Gen Z adults today identify as religious, compared with 19% of Millennials, 22% of Gen X and 18% of Boomers.
- Gen Z is also the least likely generation to identify as neither religious nor spiritual (19%).
- 88% of Gen Z regularly participate in at least one religious or spiritual practice, the highest share of any generation.
- Gen Z is more likely than Boomers to regularly read religious texts and attend religious services.
- 56% of Gen Z say they have turned to manifestation practices or spirituality to feel greater control over their future: 69% have learned a new skill or pursued training, 62% have started a creative project, 59% have restructured work to fit the life they want, and 57% have shown up more for their local community.
- 70% of Gen Z want to belong to more real-world, in-person communities, including run clubs, faith communities, hobbies and volunteer groups.”


**CONFIDENCE UP, CONTROL DOWN**


Recession fears are easing, yet more than one in four Americans don’t feel in control of their day-to-day finances, according to September’s Financial Resilience Index from Harris Poll and[NerdWallet](https://www.nerdwallet.com/finance/studies/financial-resilience-index) .


- 27% of Americans say they do not feel in control of their day-to-day finances, up from 23% in July.
- Recession expectations fell from 66% in May to 61% in September, yet the share feeling financially in control dropped from 77% in July to 73% today.
- 78% are confident they can pay all their bills on time this month.
- 63% have enough cash to cover an unexpected $1,000 expense.
- Parents (44%) are more likely than nonparents (31%) to rely on credit to make ends meet.
- Financial confidence declines by age: 89% of Boomers are confident they can pay bills on time, compared with 68% of Gen Z.
- *See also:*[Nearly half (46%) of frontline workers resort to borrowing money between pay periods](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/new-research-on-frontline-workers-finds-widening-expectation-gap-in-schedule-flexibility-pay-clarity-and-digital-tools-302881508.html)


**RESPONSIBLE AI**


While job seekers overwhelmingly feel AI-ready, hiring managers want candidates to demonstrate they also can use AI responsibly, communicate its outputs and understand its risks, according to The Harris Poll and[Express Employment Professionals](https://www.expresspros.com/newsroom/news-releases/news-releases/2026/09/93-percent-of-job-seekers-say-they-are-ai-ready-but-41-percent-of-employers-expect-advanced-skills) .


- 9 in 10 hiring managers look for candidates with at least basic AI skills.
- 93% of job seekers say they’re AI-ready, yet only 35% think employers want advanced skills – versus 41% of hiring managers who do.
- For employers, AI readiness means understanding data privacy and security (45%) and clearly communicating AI outputs (45%).
- 37% of hiring managers prioritize candidates’ understanding of bias and fairness in AI.
- Half of Gen Z (50%) and Millennials (55%) rate their own AI skills as advanced or expert, compared with 31% of Gen X and 12% of Boomers.
- Men (42%) are more likely than women (28%) to expect employers to seek advanced AI skills.
- *See also:*[AI failures often trace back to poor data foundation](https://www.ciodive.com/news/ai-failures-link-poor-data-foundation-survey/830729/)


**CONVENIENCE STORES CONVERT**


Convenience stores are high-intent retail destinations, not just quick pit stops, where shoppers linger and reliably make purchases, according to new research from Stagwell Marketing Cloud’s[Numetrix](https://www.numetrix.io/resources/convenience-store-shopping-behavior-dooh-retail-media?utm_campaign=54116907-Convenience%20Store%20Report%202026&utm_source=email&utm_content=rayday) .


- 98% of consumers who enter a convenience store make a purchase, spending $22.93 per trip on average.
- The average visit lasts 5.92 minutes, while 63% of visits run four minutes or longer.
- 56% enter primarily to buy something to eat or drink, compared with 19.2% who enter to pay for fuel.
- Shoppers visit frequently, as 93% made multiple convenience-store trips in the prior four weeks, averaging 6.8 visits.
- 91% make impulse purchases at least sometimes.
